Institute of Neurology 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr Ahmed  
St Mary's Hospital  
Institute of Neurology, St Mary's Hospital, London W2 1NY  

Dear Dr Ahmed,  

Thomas Reid, DOB: 12-04-1986, Hospital No: R518203 NHS No. 9843216750  
23 Gardeners Row, London, W10 5PL 

Medication: 

Levetiracetam 1 g twice daily.  
Clobazam 10 mg at night as needed for clusters.  
Vagus Nerve Stimulator (VNS) active; patient-initiated magnet use.  
Rescue: Buccolam 10 mg buccal as directed for prolonged clusters. 

I reviewed Thomas Reid in clinic today. He works outdoors in gardening and groundskeeping, noting that heat and prolonged exertion vary by season and can make him feel more fatigued on summer afternoons. He has been careful with hydration and pacing, and he takes brief shade breaks when feasible. He does not drive. 

His seizures typically occur in clusters, generally spaced four days apart, though brief periods of daily seizures have been reported. VNS is used more frequently, and Buccolam was administered once each month over the past 4 months. He reports that clusters are more likely after consecutive long days in hot weather; during cooler weeks he experiences fewer daytime events and relies less on the VNS magnet. Night-time rest has improved since adopting earlier bedtimes on work nights. There have been no injuries, and postictal recovery is usually under an hour. 

He feels Levetiracetam is well tolerated without mood change. Clobazam is kept for early cluster signs, especially when he anticipates multiple consecutive outdoor shifts. He has a clear rescue plan at work: a colleague is aware of Buccolam location and when to contact emergency services. No missed doses reported. 

We discussed practical measures he is already using at work—regular fluid intake, lighter tasks during peak heat when possible, and scheduled breaks. He will continue to record seizure timing relative to shift length, ambient temperature, and hydration, which may help us refine strategies. He will also note magnet use and any Buccolam doses. 

Examination today was unremarkable. Weight stable; no concerns raised regarding skin integrity or dehydration. VNS site looks healthy with no local tenderness. 

Plan: 
- Continue Levetiracetam 1 g twice daily.  
- Continue access to Clobazam 10 mg at night for clusters as currently used.  
- Maintain VNS magnet strategy and workplace rescue protocol with Buccolam available.  
- Keep detailed seizure and trigger diary including work conditions (heat/exertion), hydration, and sleep.  
- We will review in four months or sooner if seizure clusters escalate or rescue medication is required more than monthly. 

We will see him back in four months. 

Yours sincerely

KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE


Clinic Date: 02 February 2019 

Dr Amelia Reid
Riverside Medical Centre

12 Wharf Street, London, SE8 3AB
Dear Dr Amelia Reid
Michael Turner, DOB: 14-02-1991, Hospital No: H829374 NHS No. 7465129380
22A Lockside Mews, London, SE8 4PL 

Thank you for referring the above patient back to the Neurology Clinic. I reviewed him today following the birth of his child within the last six months. He reports that night-time sleep has been fragmented since the baby arrived, with multiple awakenings most nights. 

He has a diagnosis of combined generalised and focal epilepsy; he and his partner describe events consistent with both generalised convulsive seizures and focal impaired awareness episodes. He identifies occasional focal auras (brief rising epigastric sensation and sudden pause in activity) that sometimes progress, and there have been intermittent generalised tonic–clonic seizures, often out of sleep.

Regarding current seizure pattern, his seizures typically occur in clusters, generally spaced four to five days apart, though brief periods of daily seizures have been reported. VNS is used more frequently, and Buccolam was administered once each month over the past 4 months. He reports that cluster occurrence appears worse after several consecutive nights of disrupted sleep. His partner keeps a diary that broadly corroborates this pattern.

Current treatment includes Levetiracetam 1500 mg b.d., Lamotrigine 200 mg b.d., and Clobazam 10 mg nocte with an additional 5–10 mg as needed for clusters on clinician advice in the past. He has an implanted Vagus Nerve Stimulator (VNS) which he swipes more often during prodromal symptoms, particularly overnight. Rescue medication is Buccolam (midazolam) oromucosal, which he has required approximately once per month over the last four months, with good effect and no reported adverse reactions other than transient drowsiness. He denies new rashes, visual disturbance, or ataxia. He notes increased daytime fatigue, which he attributes to poor sleep and cumulative medication effects. 

Examination today was unremarkable. Neurological examination was non-focal. Observations were stable. No tongue lacerations or injuries reported since the last visit. 

We discussed the likely contribution of sleep fragmentation to seizure clustering. He remains motivated to continue VNS use and maintain a seizure diary. He has not driven. We reviewed SUDEP awareness and general safety measures, particularly around infant care and night-time supervision. He and his partner have put in place practical strategies (monitoring and alternating night duties) and feel these are helping. 

Plan:
- Continue Levetiracetam 1500 mg b.d., Lamotrigine 200 mg b.d., and Clobazam 10 mg nocte with previously advised as-needed dosing for clusters.
- Continue VNS with magnet use at aura or early cluster onset as currently practised.
- Maintain seizure and sleep diary to document cluster timing relative to sleep disruption.
- Reinforce rescue protocol with Buccolam as previously instructed; partner is confident in administration.
- Arrange ambulatory EEG to sample nocturnal periods given concern for sleep-related exacerbation.
- Refer to epilepsy specialist nurse for counselling on sleep hygiene and practical seizure management in the post-partum context.
- Safety advice reiterated; he is not driving and will continue to adhere to DVLA guidance.

I will review him in three months or sooner if clusters escalate or rescue medication is required more frequently than current use. Please let me know if there are any concerns in the interim.

Yours sincerely

Department of Neurology 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr Patel  
St George’s University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust  
Department of Neurology, Blackshaw Road, London SW17 0QT  

Dear Dr Patel,  

Emily Carter, DOB: 14-02-1992, Hospital No: H473920 NHS No. 9384756201  
Flat 12, 28 Wandsworth Road, London, SW8 2LG 

Diagnoses: 

Recurrent epileptic seizures of uncertain classification; possible catamenial association based on patient-reported menstrual tracking app entries.

Current Medication: 

- Levetiracetam 1 g bd  
- Clobazam 10 mg nocte (intermittent use per seizure clusters)  
- Buccolam (midazolam) oromucosal 10 mg for prolonged seizures as per rescue protocol  
- Vagus Nerve Stimulator in situ (implanted 2023)

Plan: 

- Continue current anti-seizure regimen unchanged at present.  
- Maintain detailed seizure and menstrual cycle tracking; patient to continue using menstrual tracking app and share exports before next review.  
- Rescue plan reaffirmed: Buccolam for prolonged events, with clear guidance to seek urgent care if clusters persist beyond usual pattern.  
- Consider perimenstrual clobazam “pulsed” strategy if pattern persists; to be reviewed at next appointment once further correlation is confirmed.  
- Check serum levetiracetam level, FBC, U&Es, LFTs, vitamin D.  
- VNS settings to be reviewed in device clinic; encourage on-demand magnet use as trained.  
- Safety advice reinforced including SUDEP risk minimisation, adherence, and avoiding known personal triggers where possible.  
- Follow up in 4 months, sooner if deterioration.

I reviewed Emily Carter in clinic today. She reports a variable pattern of seizures over recent months, and has been keeping a detailed diary alongside a menstrual tracking app. The entries suggest clustering around specific cycle phases, and she will continue to track this to help clarify any catamenial association. His seizures typically occur in clusters, generally spaced 5 days apart, though brief periods of daily seizures have been reported. VNS is used more frequently, and Buccolam was administered once each month over the past 3 months. There have been no injuries, and recovery has been quicker when on-demand VNS is applied promptly.

She feels that sleep disruption and acute stress may contribute, and has started consistent sleep and hydration routines. She is tolerating levetiracetam without mood change, and uses clobazam intermittently during anticipated clusters. There are no current plans for pregnancy; preconception counselling was briefly discussed should this change.

I have advised continuation of current therapy and reinforced the rescue plan. We will obtain blood tests today and arrange a VNS device check. Should the cycle-linked pattern be confirmed over the next two cycles, we will discuss a short perimenstrual clobazam strategy at review. She understands to seek urgent help for prolonged seizures, repeated clusters without recovery, or any new focal neurological deficits.

With best wishes,

University College Hospital 

National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery 

Clinic Date: 20 February 2024 

Dr Helen Carter  
Highgate Group Practice  
92 Dartmouth Park Hill, London NW5 1HL  

Dear Dr Helen Carter,  

Mark Thompson, DOB: 22-07-1984, Hospital No: T948210 NHS No. 3849201756  
Flat 3, 41 Lyndhurst Road, London, N19 5BQ 

Summary/ Diagnoses: Epilepsy with prior periods of variable seizure control; history of low mood under community team follow-up; vitamin D insufficiency on supplementation; ex-smoker. Marked improvement on current medicines compared with earlier periods. 

Medication: 
- Levetiracetam 1,500 mg twice daily. 
- Lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily. 
- Vitamin D3 1,000 IU once daily. 
- Omeprazole 20 mg once daily. 

I reviewed Mark in clinic today, accompanied by his sister who helps coordinate appointments. Since initiation and careful titration of the above antiepileptic regimen through late 2023, both he and his family report better day-to-day steadiness, improved concentration, and fewer post-event headaches. He is sleeping more regularly, has resumed short daily walks, and has restarted a part-time volunteering role at a local charity shop. Appetite has normalised and weight has been stable. No adverse effects reported beyond occasional morning lethargy, which resolves after breakfast. Blood pressure and pulse were within target in clinic; general neurological examination was unchanged with no new focal signs. 

Seizures: We reviewed the carer-kept diary and respite care logs. He had a cluster of three seizures in August (short, not full convulsions, fluctuating awareness, self-terminating). In November he had a nocturnal seizure, and in February a single tonic seizure was recorded during respite care. This represents a reduction compared with his pattern earlier last year when events were more frequent and recovery slower. There have been no injuries, no status episodes, and no emergency department attendances. Triggers appear to correlate with sleep disruption; alcohol remains abstinent. 

Plan: 
- Continue current antiepileptic medicines unchanged given clear clinical improvement. 
- Reinforce sleep hygiene and regular routines; family have a written plan they find helpful. 
- Safety: continue use of a soft headboard and supervised bathing; no driving. 
- Bloods: U&E, LFT, FBC, vitamin D and levetiracetam trough level to be checked at your practice in the next 2–3 weeks; please forward results. 
- Follow-up with our epilepsy nurse by telephone in 3 months, and consultant review in 6 months or sooner if seizure frequency increases or events change in character. 

Yours sincerely

St Mary's Hospital 

Institute of Neurology 

Clinic Date: 7 October 2011 

Dr Patel  
St Mary's Hospital  
Institute of Neurology, St Mary's Hospital, London W2 1NY  

Dear Dr Patel,  

Sophie Bennett, DOB: 12-03-1998, Hospital No: H938420 NHS No. 5837201496  
14 Brookfield Road, London, W10 5PR 

Medication: 

Lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily, continued. Tolerated well with stable mood and no reported rash. Menstrual-related pattern improved under the existing approach. 

I reviewed Sophie Bennett in clinic today for known focal epilepsy. She reports a steady improvement overall with fewer events and shorter duration when they do occur. The family have kept a simple diary, which supports this trajectory. In Apr she experienced four short absences in a cluster (self-limited). In Jul there was 2 further brief absences, and in Sep another at school (not witnessed by family). There have been no convulsions, no injuries, and recovery has been rapid after each brief episode. She and her parents feel control is better compared to earlier in the year, and there has been no deterioration with school return. 

The semiology remains consistent with focal onset: brief behavioural arrest with staring and loss of contact for seconds, occasional right-hand fidgeting, and prompt return to baseline without post-ictal confusion. No nocturnal events have been reported. She continues to identify menses as a prior trigger; however, with the current regimen and routine sleep measures, the perimenstrual clustering has lessened and the last cycle passed without events. 

Examination today was normal. There are no adverse effects of medication reported, and adherence is good. We discussed usual safety advice including sleep regularity and illness management; no changes in school activity are required. 

Plan: continue Lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily unchanged. Keep seizure diary and note temporal relation to menses. We will monitor for any return of clustering; at present, given the improvement and absence of functional impact, no dose adjustment is indicated. 

Follow-up in six months, sooner if there is any escalation in frequency, injury, or change in semiology. 

Yours sincerely

University College Hospital 

National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery 

Clinic Date: 7 November 2023 

Dr A. Patel  
Riverside Medical Practice  
12 Wharf Road, London N1 7RW  

Dear Dr A. Patel,  

John Miller, DOB: 22-04-1982, Hospital No: U784512 NHS No. 1039485712  
Flat 3, 47 Kingfisher Court, London, SE10 8AL 

Summary/ Diagnoses: Focal epilepsy with recent clinical deterioration/new event phenotype reported/left frontal gliosis post-meningitis (2019)/generalised anxiety disorder/GERD/osteopenia/smoker (rolling tobacco ~5/day). 

Medication: Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily.  
Levetiracetam 1,500 mg twice daily.  
Omeprazole 20 mg once daily.  
Sertraline 50 mg once daily.  
Calcium/Vitamin D supplementation.  

I reviewed John in clinic today accompanied by his partner, who keeps a diary. He describes a clear change in his habitual events over the last three months, with features not present in prior descriptions. Previously his focal seizures were rare, brief, and stereotyped with right-hand tingling and preserved awareness. Since late summer he has noticed nocturnal events, occasional head deviation, and post-event confusion lasting 20–40 minutes, which is a new event phenotype when compared with his baseline pattern. He also reports new morning myalgia and tongue soreness on two occasions. There have been no clear triggers identified, though sleep fragmentation and recent work stress were noted. 

Seizures: He had a cluster of three seizures in Aug (short, not full convulsions, fluctuating awareness, self-terminating). In Sep he had six nocturnal seizures, and in Oct a single tonic seizure was recorded during respite care. These reports come from the partner-held diary and a respite unit incident form. Overall, this reflects a deterioration from his prior low-frequency focal seizures. 

Examination: Alert and oriented, speech fluent. Cranial nerves intact. Motor: full power throughout, no pronator drift. Sensation grossly intact. Coordination normal. Gait narrow-based but steady. No focal neurological deficit identified today. 

Investigations to date: Last lamotrigine and levetiracetam levels checked March 2023 (within reference). MRI brain (2021) demonstrated left frontal gliosis without progression; routine EEG (2020) showed left frontotemporal sharp waves. No recent bloods available from primary care. 

Assessment: Focal epilepsy with a clinically significant deterioration and emergence of a new event phenotype suggestive of evolving focal to bilateral risk. The pattern of nocturnal events and a documented tonic seizure at respite signify increased seizure burden compared with his prior course. 

Plan: 
- Safety: Reinforced SUDEP and safety counselling; advised strict nocturnal supervision measures and seizure alarm use as discussed. Driving: not driving and remains unfit to drive; DVLA guidance reiterated. 
- Medication: Continue levetiracetam 1,500 mg twice daily and lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily pending levels. We will consider lamotrigine uptitration versus adjunct lacosamide after results and EEG review. 
- Tests: Request urgent anti-seizure medication trough levels, U&E, LFT, FBC, vitamin D. Arrange sleep-deprived EEG and ambulatory EEG to capture nocturnal events. Book updated MRI brain with epilepsy protocol given new semiology. 
- Triggers/Wellbeing: Emphasised sleep regularity, alcohol avoidance (he denies current alcohol), and stress management; offered referral to epilepsy nurse specialist for seizure action plan and diary review. 
- Follow-up: Early review in 6–8 weeks or sooner if further clusters occur. Partner to continue detailed event diary and, where feasible, obtain brief video during events. 

Yours sincerely

Centre for Neurology Services

Neurosciences Division 

Clinic Date: 4 March 2026 

Dr Aisha Rahman 
Consultant Neurologist  
Riverside Neurology Centre  
St Anne’s Wing, Meadowview Hospital, Brighton  

Dear Dr Aisha Rahman,

Alex Morgan, DOB: 22-07-1987, Hospital No: B9142736 NHS No. 4482097163  
12 Parkside Close, Hove, BN3 4QA  

Diagnosis:

Seizure disorder; current classification not specified. Prior treatment response variable across agents.

Aetiology:

No definitive structural, genetic, or metabolic cause identified to date. Previous MRI and routine EEG unremarkable per prior records.

Other Medical Problems:

Generalised anxiety symptoms related to travel (notably air travel). Mild vitamin D insufficiency on supplementation.

Background and Current Status:

The patient reports that a previous seizure occurred during air travel, which has contributed to travel-related anxiety; they have since limited flying and have adopted practical coping strategies. Since the last review, the following events were recorded: In September a prolonged focal seizure (~10 minutes) settled spontaneously. In November a tonic seizure were recorded, and in February another during physiotherapy. No clear prodrome was noted for the September episode; the November event occurred after a poor night’s sleep; the February event followed exertion during rehabilitation exercises. There have been no reported injuries. Rescue medication has not yet been required in the community setting.

Medication History and Tolerability:

- Levetiracetam previously tried with mood-related adverse effects; discontinued.
- Lamotrigine previously trialled; unclear benefit at moderate dose; discontinued after shared decision-making.
- Currently on lacosamide 100 mg twice daily with acceptable tolerability; occasional dizziness on rapid postural change.
- Vitamin D3 1000 IU daily.

Management Plan:

- Continue lacosamide 100 mg twice daily without change today; reinforce adherence and hydration advice around physiotherapy sessions.
- Provide a written seizure action plan for use at home and in physiotherapy settings; issue rescue buccal midazolam for prolonged events, with training for family and physiotherapy staff.
- Arrange ambulatory EEG to seek interictal correlates; consider sleep-deprived protocol given the November event after sleep deprivation.
- Repeat MRI brain with epilepsy protocol to reassess for subtle lesions not identified previously.
- Discuss graded re-introduction to air travel only if the patient wishes, alongside practical measures to address travel anxiety; offer referral to psychology for brief CBT-based strategies targeting anticipatory anxiety.
- Safety counselling updated: bathing/showering guidance, sports/physiotherapy precautions, and driving regulations reviewed in accordance with DVLA guidance.
- Bloods: FBC, U&E, LFT, vitamin D level, and lacosamide trough in 6 weeks.
- Follow-up in 4 months, sooner if further events occur or adverse effects develop.

Work and Daily Function:

The patient remains employed and reports manageable fatigue post-physiotherapy. They have informed their employer regarding episodic events occurring around exertion; a flexible schedule for therapy sessions has been agreed.

Yours sincerely,

St Mary's Hospital 

Institute of Neurology 

Clinic Date: 9 May 2017 

Dr Ahmed  
St Mary's Hospital  
Institute of Neurology, St Mary's Hospital, London W2 1NY  

Dear Dr Ahmed,  

Mateo Alvarez, DOB: 14-03-1986, Hospital No: H938271 NHS No. 5839201746  
12 Brookfield Road, London, W10 5RA 

Medication: 

Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily, commenced following initial assessment in primary care after recent events. Patient reports good adherence, with occasional missed morning doses during shift work. No notable adverse effects beyond mild irritability in the first fortnight, now settled. 

History and interval events: 

Mateo Alvarez is a recent migrant to the UK and is still learning how to navigate NHS services; he has occasionally attended with interpreter support. He has received our written safety advice translated into his preferred language and confirms understanding. Since initial review by the GP, the pattern of episodes has been clarified as follows: In November he presented with a cluster of three seizures (self-terminating, fluctuating awareness). In February a nocturnal seizure were noted, and in April a single generalised tonic-clonic seizure occurred (not witnessed by family). No clear precipitants identified; he reports variable sleep due to new employment and some stress around housing paperwork. There is no history of significant head injury, CNS infection, or family history of similar episodes. 

Examination today is unremarkable with normal cardiorespiratory and neurological findings. He is oriented, with no focal deficits. 

Investigations: 

- Baseline bloods in primary care reported as within reference ranges (U&E, LFT, FBC).  
- We have arranged a routine EEG and MRI brain with epilepsy protocol; appointments have been requested with attention to interpreter availability.  
- DVLA guidance and safety precautions (bathing/swimming supervision, heights, machinery) discussed and provided in writing; he confirms he will refrain from driving and has initiated self-notification.  

Plan: 

1) Continue levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily for now; we will review dosing after EEG/MRI and in light of any further events.  
2) Seizure diary provided; he will record sleep patterns, missed doses, and any alcohol intake to help identify triggers.  
3) Written first aid guidance shared with family; he has consented to us sending a summary to his workplace occupational health.  
4) Interpreter-supported follow-up booked for 12 weeks, sooner if further seizures occur or adverse effects develop.  
5) Signposted to local community support and an information session on accessing NHS appointments, including how to request interpreters in advance.  

We will update you when investigations are available. Please contact us if there are interim concerns or if further events occur. 

Yours sincerely

Centre for Epilepsy

Neurosciences Division 

Clinic Date: 23 August 2010 

Dr Sarah Ahmed 
Consultant Neurologist  
Centre for Epilepsy  
St. Bartholomew’s Hospital, London  

Dear Dr Sarah Ahmed, 

Emma Carter, DOB: 12-06-1996, Hospital No: A837462 NHS No. 2045891173  
Flat 3, 22 Brook Lane, London, SE5 9QH  

Diagnosis: 

Focal epilepsy with good response to Lamotrigine; Levetiracetam previously ineffective; Phenytoin not tolerated due to dizziness and cognitive slowing.

Aetiology: 

Perinatal infarct affecting the right parietal region (radiologically stable on prior imaging).

Other Medical Problems: 

Vitamin D insufficiency on supplementation; mild migraine without aura; no known drug allergies.

Background and Recent Events: 

She wears a smartwatch with fall-detection enabled; the device logs have been useful in corroborating the timing of events when available. In Mar she experienced a prolonged focal seizure lasting 8 minutes, resolving without intervention. In May there were three further brief absences, and in Aug a single generalised tonic-clonic seizure was reported at school (not witnessed by family). The school nurse documented a post-ictal phase of approximately 15 minutes; the smartwatch registered a hard fall alert at the corresponding time. There have been no emergency department attendances, and there has been no reported injury.

Current Treatment: 

Lamotrigine 150 mg mane and 200 mg nocte, single brand only. Buccal midazolam rescue pack held at school and home but not administered during the above events.

Management Plan: 

- Continue Lamotrigine at current dosing and maintain single-brand supply to avoid variability.  
- Arrange serum Lamotrigine level and vitamin D recheck prior to next review.  
- School has been provided with updated seizure first-aid guidance; smartwatch fall alerts to be printed from the companion app to support event chronology.  
- No driving. Occupational advice provided regarding graded return to PE participation at school with supervision.

Summary: 

This patient has focal epilepsy attributed to a perinatal parietal infarct. Event chronology over the past six months is as above, with smartwatch data aiding correlation of timings. No medication changes are proposed today given overall tolerability and absence of clustering or status features. I will review in six months or sooner if further generalised events occur.

Yours sincerely

Dr Kate
Health Centre

Keele University, Keele, Newcastle

Staffordshire ST5 5BG
Dear Dr Kate
Amelia Jones, DOB: 12-03-1994, Hospital No: K593021 NHS No. 7483926150
12 Orchard Mews, Newcastle-under-Lyme, ST5 1AB 

Diagnoses/summary: Generalised epilepsy with history of childhood febrile seizures; current clinical focus is adult epilepsy management. No known structural brain abnormality on prior imaging (patient-reported MRI in 2017 normal). Family history negative for epilepsy. No learning disability. No known cardiac history.

Previous medication: Sodium valproate (discontinued due to weight gain and tremor), levetiracetam (mood irritability), clonazepam PRN for clusters, ethosuximide in childhood (for absences).

In March she had a drop attack, and in May five myoclonic jerks were documented at college (not observed directly by parents). She denies intercurrent illness or missed doses around these events. No injuries apart from minor bruising with the March episode. She reports early morning myoclonus about once weekly otherwise, and occasional brief absences per her description (brief staring with rapid recovery), though not all have been witnessed.

Current medication: Levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily (self-reduced to 750 mg in the morning for two weeks due to irritability, now back to 1000 mg BD), folic acid 400 micrograms daily, vitamin D 1000 IU daily. No contraception interactions anticipated; she uses a copper IUD. She does not drive.

Examination: General and neurological examination today was normal. Weight stable; BMI 23.4. No focal deficits. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations unremarkable.

Investigations: Routine EEG in 2019 reportedly showed generalised spike-and-wave bursts with photoparoxysmal response (report seen). No recent bloods; we will check U&E, LFT, FBC, vitamin D, and TSH.

Discussion: We discussed that her pattern is consistent with generalised epilepsy, with variable myoclonus and probable absences; the December event suggests secondary generalisation or a longer generalised tonic–clonic seizure with fluctuating semiology as per witness account. Mood side effects on levetiracetam remain a concern. We reviewed treatment options including switching to or adding lamotrigine or topiramate, and non-pharmacological measures (sleep regularity, alcohol avoidance, adherence). We also discussed SUDEP risk reduction strategies and seizure first aid with her partner.

Plan:
- Transition plan to lamotrigine: initiate 25 mg once daily for 2 weeks, then 25 mg twice daily for 2 weeks, then 50 mg twice daily, aiming for 100 mg twice daily as tolerated. We will then consider tapering levetiracetam depending on response.
- Provide written titration schedule and adverse effect counselling (rash/Stevens–Johnson, dizziness, ataxia). She understands to seek urgent advice if rash develops.
- Rescue plan: clonazepam 0.5 mg orally for clusters of myoclonus or prolonged absence sequences, maximum 1 mg in 24 hours; partner instructed regarding when to call 999 (convulsive seizure >5 minutes, repeated seizures without recovery, injury).
- Blood tests today: FBC, U&E, LFT, TSH, vitamin D.
- Safety: reinforced avoidance of swimming alone, heights, and open flames; continue not driving in line with DVLA guidance.
- Follow-up: nurse specialist telephone review in 4 weeks to assess tolerability and diary; clinic review in 3 months, sooner if deterioration.

Thank you for your ongoing care and for prescribing lamotrigine per the above titration if local protocol permits. Please let me know if there are any concerns.

Yours sincerely

Department of Neurology

Clinic Date: 11 February 2016

Dr Amelia Green
St Helier Neurology Clinic
Epsom and St Helier University Hospitals, Neurology Department, Wrythe Lane, Carshalton SM5 1AA

Dear Dr Amelia Green,

Emily Carter, DOB: 14-03-2001, Hospital No: H927451 NHS No. 6031847295
29 Meadowbank Close, Sutton, SM2 6QL

Diagnoses:

Recurrent seizures of uncertain classification; prior EEG non-diagnostic.

Current Medication:

Lamotrigine 75 mg bd

Plan:

Continue current antiepileptic therapy; reinforce seizure first-aid education; maintain seizure diary; routine follow-up in 12 months or earlier if further events occur.

I reviewed Emily Carter in clinic today. She attended with her mother, who provided additional collateral history. She has previously practised aura recognition strategies with our epilepsy nurse team and continues to describe warning features in her own words as a "hollow, rising feeling in the chest with a brief sense of detachment" lasting 10–20 seconds, typically occurring before more obvious events. Over the last several months there has been a variable pattern of episodes: In August she experienced a prolonged focal seizure lasting 8 minutes, resolving without intervention. In October there were two further brief absences, and in January a single generalised tonic-clonic seizure was reported at school (not witnessed by family). She reports good adherence to Lamotrigine 75 mg twice daily and denies missed doses.

She and her mother have kept a diary noting sleep disruption as a possible trigger. There is no recent intercurrent illness, alcohol exposure, or new medications. Neurological examination in clinic today was normal. There is no injury history from the January event, and recovery was described as gradual but complete within several hours. There is no consistent diurnal pattern reported.

We discussed ongoing management. She finds the aura recognition techniques helpful to prompt sitting down, alerting staff, and ensuring a safe environment. She understands standard seizure first-aid and the school has a care plan. We agreed to continue Lamotrigine 75 mg twice daily without dose change for now, as tolerability remains good and there are no reported adverse effects (no rash, mood change, or dizziness). I have asked her to maintain a detailed diary, including aura descriptions, potential triggers, and any witness reports from school. We will also request updated school incident documentation to clarify semiology where available.

I have arranged routine follow-up in 12 months, with open access to earlier review if there are further prolonged events, clusters, or any injuries. She was given advice on sleep hygiene and safety, including supervision around water and avoidance of heights when a warning is present.

With best wishes,

KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE


Clinic Date: 8 September 2010 

Dr Patel
Elmwood Medical Centre

72 Elmwood Road, London, SE5 3HT
Dear Dr Patel
Jane Smith, DOB: 21-11-1982, Hospital No: H738291 NHS No. 0093384721
Flat 4, 21 Brook Lane, London, SE5 1AB 

Thank you for asking me to review the above patient in the Neurology Clinic today. She is known to our service with focal epilepsy and, encouragingly, reports a steady improvement over recent months, which she attributes to better adherence following use of a consistent seizure diary and reminders on her phone.

Current treatment consists of Lamotrigine 150 mg b.d. and Levetiracetam 1 g b.d., both well tolerated without dose-limiting adverse effects. She reports improved energy levels compared to earlier in the year and no new intercurrent illnesses. There is no current concern regarding mood or sleep beyond occasional pre-examination anxiety, which she manages with standard breathing techniques taught by our epilepsy nurse specialist.

Regarding recent events: In February she experienced a prolonged focal seizure lasting 8 minutes, resolving without intervention. In May there were four further brief absences, and in August a single generalised tonic-clonic seizure was reported at school (not witnessed by family). These episodes have been clearly recorded in her diary, with triggers likely related to missed meals and sleep deprivation around coursework deadlines. Since adopting structured reminders in late August, she has had no further events and has taken all doses on time.

Neurological examination today is unremarkable. There are no drug-related rashes, no tremor, and no cognitive concerns on bedside screening. We discussed safety and rescue planning; no rescue medication has been required. She prefers to avoid changes while her control is improving, and I agree that stability is prudent given the recent positive trajectory.

Plan:
- Continue Lamotrigine 150 mg b.d. and Levetiracetam 1 g b.d. unchanged.
- Maintain seizure diary and phone reminders; continue avoidance of sleep deprivation and missed meals.
- Bloods today for routine monitoring (FBC, U&Es, LFTs) – to be copied to you.
- Review in clinic in 4 months, sooner if breakthrough seizures recur or if tolerability issues arise.

Overall, her focal epilepsy appears better controlled with improved adherence, and she is optimistic about maintaining this trajectory.

Yours sincerely

typed_input.note_text:
Centre for Epilepsy

Neurosciences Division 

Clinic Date: 3 October 2015 

Dr Anita Shah 
Consultant Neurologist  
Centre for Epilepsy  
Kingston Hospital NHS Foundation Trust  

Dear Dr Anita Shah, 

Alex Morgan, DOB: 22-08-1992, Hospital No: K847210 NHS No. 3014729986  
Flat 12, 9 Riverbank Way, Kingston upon Thames, KT1 2AB  

Diagnosis: 

Generalised epilepsy with recent clusters of brief seizures; valproate responsive but with residual breakthrough episodes

Aetiology: 

Presumed genetic generalised epilepsy; no structural lesion identified; normal development and no perinatal complications

Other Medical Problems: 

Generalised anxiety and low mood, patient reports intermittent sleep disturbance and health-related worry; no self-harm; currently engaged with GP for talking therapy referral

Management Plan: 

- Continue sodium valproate modified release 500 mg mane and 1000 mg nocte.  
- Introduce rescue plan for clusters: buccal midazolam 5 mg if three or more brief seizures occur within 30 minutes, or if a seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes; mother instructed and provided written guidance.  
- Sleep hygiene advice and stress-management strategies discussed; encourage ongoing counselling via IAPT.  
- Safety advice: avoid sleep deprivation, limit alcohol, and adhere to DVLA guidance for seizures.  
- Arrange ambulatory EEG and serum valproate level prior to next visit; routine bloods including FBC, LFTs.  
- Review in four months, earlier if further clusters occur.

This patient has generalised epilepsy and describes variable brief events without consistent focal onset features. In April he had a run of 6 seizures within half an hour (not full generalised tonic-clonic, fluctuating in intensity, resolved without medication). In June there was six further seizures at night, and in September another during physiotherapy (unwitnessed by mother). He did not require emergency care and there has been no associated injury. He links the periods of increased seizure activity to poor sleep and heightened anxiety. Valproate has otherwise reduced background events, and there have been no prolonged generalised tonic–clonic seizures for over a year. We discussed a pragmatic rescue plan for clusters, reinforcement of adherence, and strategies to address anxiety and sleep, as these appear to act as triggers. No adverse effects from valproate reported; weight stable and mood symptoms predate treatment. I will update you following the EEG and blood results.

Yours sincerely

Department of Neurology 

Clinic Date: 15 May 2011 

Dr Amelia Grant  
St. Bartholomew’s Hospital  
Department of Neurology, West Smithfield, London EC1A 7BE  

Dear Dr Amelia Grant,  

Michael Turner, DOB: 22-03-1976, Hospital No: H392744 NHS No. 9045127763  
Flat 2, 18 Brookside Lane, Enfield, London EN2 7QX 

Diagnoses: 

Recurrent seizures of unclear classification; prior normal neuroimaging (2010); no clear precipitant identified.

Current Medication: 

Levetiracetam 500 mg bd  
Clobazam 5 mg nocte prn for clusters

Plan: 

- Continue levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily.  
- Safety advice reinforced for outdoor manual work in heat and during prolonged exertion; patient to take regular shaded breaks and maintain hydration.  
- Driving advice per DVLA guidance discussed and understood.  
- Arrange repeat EEG and ambulatory ECG to explore reported drop attacks.  
- Follow up in 4 months, or sooner if further events occur.

I reviewed Michael Turner in clinic today. He works in gardening and groundskeeping outdoors, where heat exposure and prolonged exertion vary seasonally. He reports that fluctuations in temperature and workload can affect his fatigue levels. Since his last appointment in November, he has kept a detailed diary of events. In Dec 3 brief absences were reported. In Mar 5 drop attacks occurred, and in Apr another tonic seizure was recorded. The absences were described as sudden pauses with unresponsiveness lasting a few seconds, without clear warning, followed by rapid recovery. The drop attacks were brief with loss of postural tone and immediate reorientation; no clear vertigo, palpitations, or prolonged confusion was noted. The tonic event in April occurred late afternoon after a long shift in warm conditions, with muscle stiffening, a fall, and tongue bite; recovery to baseline took around 30 minutes according to a colleague.

There have been no head injuries requiring hospital attendance. He denies alcohol excess and has been sleeping 7–8 hours on most nights, though notes early starts during spring workload peaks. He has not identified consistent auras. Medication adherence has been good; no missed doses reported. There are no new neurological symptoms between events. Routine bloods in March (U&E, LFTs, FBC) were within reference ranges. Prior MRI brain (March 2010) was unremarkable.

Given the variety of event types and the occupational context, I have advised ongoing adherence to current treatment, attention to hydration, rest breaks, and avoidance of lone work at height or near machinery when fatigued. We discussed escalation options if further events occur before review, and he will contact the service if frequency increases or injuries occur. An EEG has been requested to characterise the brief absences, and ambulatory ECG arranged to exclude arrhythmic causes for the drop attacks.

With best wishes,

typed_input.note_text:
Epilepsy Centre 

Neurosciences Division 

Clinic Date: 8 April 2013 

Dr Patel  
North London Neurosciences Centre  
Neurology Department, 14 Highgate Hill, London N19 5LW  

Dear Dr Patel,  

Michael Harris, DOB: 28-02-1981, Hospital No: K593024 NHS No. 7482103659  
3A Wren Court, Holloway Road, London N7 6RT  

Diagnoses: 

Focal epilepsy, likely frontal onset, with nocturnal predominance.

I reviewed Michael Harris in our epilepsy clinic today by scheduled telephone appointment, which he prefers given his frequent international business travel and irregular sleep across time zones. He reports generally good adherence to lamotrigine, with occasional delayed evening doses when flying long-haul. He has been using a mobile app to track time zone changes and dosing times, which appears to have reduced missed doses. He denies adverse effects beyond occasional transient dizziness when sleep-deprived. There is no current use of rescue medication and he has not required emergency services since last year.

Seizure history since the last review: In November he had a run of one seizure within half an hour (not full generalised tonic-clonic, fluctuating in intensity, resolved without medication). In December there was 7 further seizures at night, and in March another during physiotherapy (unwitnessed by mother). He associates the November and December events with multiple red-eye flights, jet lag and fragmented sleep. The March episode followed a strenuous rehabilitation session for a minor ankle injury while he was mildly sleep-deprived; there was no reported trauma, tongue biting or incontinence. Post-ictal confusion, when present, is brief. He continues to describe a reliable focal aware aura of a rising epigastric sensation and brief speech arrest, sometimes progressing to impaired awareness; secondary generalisation has not been reported during this interval.

Examination is not applicable today as this was a telephone consultation. Review of prior investigations: MRI brain (last year) was structurally normal; routine EEG showed intermittent right frontal sharp activity with increased expression during drowsiness. No changes to his cardiac or metabolic profiles have been noted by his GP in recent blood tests. 

Plan: 
- Continue lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily. We discussed setting dual time-zone alarms to anchor dosing to home time for flights exceeding 6 hours, shifting by 1–2 hours per day to avoid large dosing gaps. 
- Provide a written travel seizure plan for airlines and hotel staff; patient to carry a copy on all trips. 
- Sleep hygiene advice emphasised, particularly avoidance of red-eye flights where feasible and limiting overnight work before major time zone changes. 
- No rescue medication indicated at present given self-limited events and absence of generalised tonic–clonic seizures; we will revisit if frequency increases. 
- Arrange ambulatory EEG if nocturnal frequency persists over the next quarter. 
- Follow-up in three months by telephone, or earlier if there is escalation, injury, or emergence of generalised tonic–clonic seizures.

Yours sincerely

St Mary's Hospital 

Institute of Neurology 

Clinic Date: 30 May 2021 

Dr Patel  
St Mary's Hospital  
Institute of Neurology, St Mary's Hospital, London W2 1NY  

Dear Dr Patel,  

George Thompson, DOB: 12-03-1941, Hospital No: H847203 NHS No. 9081726345  
Roseview Care Home, 14 Brookside Road, London, W2 5RE 

Medication:  
Levetiracetam 750 mg twice daily via crushed tablets in semi-solid; Clobazam 5 mg nocte. Both are being administered by the live-in nurse as per blister pack. No adverse effects reported beyond mild daytime somnolence, which the caregiver feels is unchanged from baseline.

Background and current status:  
George Thompson is an older adult who has been largely bedbound since a hip fracture last year. Most of the clinical history and observations are provided by his daytime nurse and overnight caregiver at the residential unit. There is no history available to suggest a single unifying trigger, and events occur from sleep and wakefulness. He does not drive. Swallow is safe for crushed medications; dietitian input is ongoing for weight maintenance.

Seizure history since the last review:  
The nursing notes and incident forms were reviewed alongside the unit’s electronic log. In Nov he had 5 short seizures in a brief series. In Feb six daytime events were noted, in Mar 5 myoclonic jerks occurred, and in May three generalised tonic-clonic seizures at the centre (staff-witnessed). The caregiver reports that post-event confusion typically lasts 10–20 minutes with gradual return to his baseline alertness. No clear illness, missed doses, or sleep deprivation were identified around these clusters. There has been no head injury, tongue biting has been recorded twice, and there was one urinary incontinence episode in May. 

Assessment and plan:  
- Continue current doses of levetiracetam and clobazam given tolerability and caregiver preference to avoid daytime sedation.  
- The unit has a rescue protocol in place (buccal midazolam 5 mg for clusters or events exceeding 5 minutes); this has not been required this quarter.  
- We have provided the caregivers with a simple event diary template and requested brief smartphone video where feasible to assist characterisation.  
- Routine bloods (FBC, U&E, LFTs) to be arranged through primary care in the next 2–4 weeks, given reduced mobility and polypharmacy.  
- Pressure area care and hydration measures to continue; the nurse will liaise with the falls team regarding safe repositioning after events.

Follow-up:  
We will review him in four months via joint video link with the nurse and caregiver, or sooner if there is any escalation in frequency, prolonged events, or new focal neurological deficits.

Yours sincerely

KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE


Clinic Date: 28 July 2014 

Dr Patel
Hillside Medical Practice

14 Hillside Road, London, SE15 2AB
Dear Dr Patel
Jane Smith, DOB: 21-11-1982, Hospital No: H728394 NHS No. 9076652319
22 Brookfield Close, London, SE15 2AD 

I reviewed the above patient in the Neurology Clinic today. She attends as the primary caregiver for her young children, and reports that night-time sleep can be interrupted due to childcare demands. She feels this has at times affected her daytime alertness and confidence, particularly on mornings after multiple awakenings.

Since her last review, she has kept a diary and provided collateral from college staff. A prolonged event occurred in Jan (approximately 12 minutes, alternating between focal and generalised features, settled spontaneously). In Apr she had a drop attack, and in Jul a myoclonic jerk were documented at college (not observed directly by parents). She did not require attendance at A&E and there was no reported injury. There are no consistent prodromes; she occasionally notes brief periods of difficulty concentrating beforehand. 

Current medication, unchanged for the past three months: Carbamazepine 400 mg b.d., Levetiracetam (Keppra) 1250 mg b.d., Topiramate 125 mg b.d., Valproate 500 mg b.d., and Clobazam 10 mg b.d. She reports tolerating this combination overall, but notes intermittent tiredness, which she attributes partly to disturbed sleep. No rash or systemic adverse effects have been observed; occasional leg itch has improved with emollients as advised by her GP. She is not driving. 

We discussed practical measures around sleep hygiene and ensuring safe supervision when fatigued. She prefers to avoid medication changes today while we clarify current event patterns. I have arranged ambulatory EEG with event button and will request a medication level profile before her next visit. She has accepted a referral to the epilepsy specialist nurse service for education and support, and we provided seizure first-aid information to college staff with her consent. 

Plan:
- Continue current medications unchanged pending investigations.
- Ambulatory EEG and serum drug levels to be arranged.
- Epilepsy specialist nurse input for education and safety planning.
- Review in clinic in 3 months, or sooner if events cluster or injuries occur.

Yours sincerely

Institute of Neurology 

Clinic Date: 21 April 2011 

Dr Ahmed  
Greenbrook Health Centre  
145 Cranford Lane, Hounslow TW5 9EX  

Dear Dr Ahmed,  

Michael Turner, DOB: 04-02-1983, Hospital No: H914276 NHS No. 8093172456  
Flat 3, Oakview Supported Living, 12 Beech Road, Hounslow TW4 6JP 

Medication: 

Levetiracetam 1 g twice daily. Staff report good adherence, no notable mood change since the last visit. Rescue midazolam oromucosal 5 mg is available in the care plan but has not been required in the period under review. 

He resides in supported accommodation where rotating staff maintain daily seizure charts and incident logs; copies were available today and used as the primary source alongside his account. He had a cluster of three seizures in Dec (short, not full convulsions, fluctuating awareness, self-terminating). In Feb he had 7 nocturnal seizures, and in Apr a single tonic seizure was recorded during respite care. There were no associated injuries documented. Post-event recovery was within 10–20 minutes on each occasion, and no emergency services were involved. 

Potential triggers noted by staff include poor sleep during room changes and increased anxiety around schedule alterations; caffeine intake has been reduced by the team with no clear effect yet. He has not had recent intercurrent illness. 

Neurological examination today is unchanged. We discussed maintaining consistent sleep routines in the residence and ensuring that new or temporary staff continue the current seizure documentation protocol. I have not altered his medication at this stage. Should the nocturnal events increase in frequency or duration, we would consider a dose optimisation of levetiracetam or alternative strategies after review of the updated charts. 

We will review him again in four months, or earlier if the supported living team identify escalation or prolonged events. 

Yours sincerely

King's College Hospital 

Department of Neurosciences 

Clinic Date: 25 December 2019 

Dr Alicia Nguyen
Consultant Neurologist  
King's College Hospital  
Department of Neurosciences, King's College Hospital, London SE5 9RS  

Dear Dr Alicia Nguyen
Consultant Neurologist,  

Sophie Patel, DOB: 14-03-1998, Hospital No: K742119 NHS No. 9075634218  
12 Grove Park Road, London, SE5 8QL

Thank you for asking me to review this patient, who attended with her mother. She is a rotating shift worker, including nights, and both she and her family report marked disruption of her circadian rhythm with variable sleep duration and frequent early morning tiredness on the weeks following night shifts. She describes intermittent brief episodes of disconnection at work and occasional startle-like twitches when overtired. There is no consistent alcohol excess. Caffeine intake fluctuates with shifts.

With regard to recent paroxysmal events, the family and patient provided a clear timeline for 2019: A prolonged event occurred in Jul (approximately 12 minutes, alternating between focal and generalised features, settled spontaneously). In Oct she had 5 drop attacks, and in Dec two myoclonic jerks were documented at college (not observed directly by parents). No injuries were sustained. She reports variable post-event fatigue but no prolonged confusion. No consistent aura is recalled. There have been no witnessed nocturnal events at home, although she often wakes unrefreshed after consecutive night duties.

Past history is unremarkable for febrile seizures, meningitis, or significant head injury. There is no known family history of seizures. She does not drive. Current medications include only a combined oral contraceptive; she is not taking any antiseizure medication. She denies recreational drug use. Mood is described as generally stable, though she notes irritability when sleep deprived. Appetite is normal. Neurological review of systems otherwise negative. On examination today she was alert and cooperative, oriented, with fluent speech. Cranial nerves intact. Motor, sensory, coordination and gait examinations were normal. No stigmata of systemic disease observed.

At present it remains difficult to ascribe a single unifying diagnosis for these events. The reported variability in semiology, the temporal clustering around periods of sleep disruption, and the lack of consistent focal neurologic signs today mean that further objective data are required. I have discussed non-prescriptive strategies she may consider to stabilise her sleep–wake schedule within the constraints of her rota, and she will keep a detailed event and sleep diary, cross-referencing shift pattern, caffeine intake, and any intercurrent illness. She and her mother are comfortable to proceed with further investigations.

Plan agreed today (patient-reported preferences included):
- Ambulatory EEG with extended montage to sample across a full shift cycle, aiming to capture events on late and night duties.
- MRI brain with epilepsy protocol to screen for a structural correlate.
- Basic bloods including FBC, U&E, LFT, calcium, magnesium, glucose, thyroid profile, vitamin D, and ferritin.
- Request contemporaneous reports from college and workplace first aid/incident logs relating to the Dec jerks and Oct drops, and any CCTV where available, to improve event characterisation.
- Safety advice regarding bathing and working at heights has been discussed in clinic terms today; she will review workplace risk assessments with her manager and occupational health. She is aware of DVLA guidance relevance should events continue.

I will review her in clinic once the above investigations are completed, or sooner if the frequency or severity of events escalates. She and her mother have our contact details for interim concerns.

Yours sincerely

KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE


Clinic Date: 23 March 2026

Dr James Cole
Riverside Health Centre

12 Avon Street, Southwark, London SE1 6TU
Dear Dr James Cole
Daniel Moore, DOB: 17-08-1994, Hospital No: H728391 NHS No. 7712039846
Flat 4, 29 Larkspur Court, London SE15 3QN 

Diagnoses/summary: Generalised epilepsy with photosensitivity; stage lighting technician with frequent exposure to strobe/bright lights; colleagues may occasionally witness events. Prior EEG reports (patient-reported) suggest generalised spike–wave discharges consistent with idiopathic generalised epilepsy. No known structural lesion.

Previous medication: Sodium valproate (effective but stopped previously due to weight gain and tremor), levetiracetam (mood irritability), lamotrigine (partial benefit), clobazam PRN for clusters (sedation), perampanel (dizziness, behavioural change), topiramate (word-finding difficulty), zonisamide (appetite suppression, low mood).

Not taken: brivaracetam, lacosamide, ethosuximide (not trialled as absence prominence uncertain), cannabidiol, rufinamide.

Comorbidities/other: Migraine without aura; mild asthma on PRN salbutamol. No known cardiac disease. No learning difficulties. Occupation: stage lighting technician; frequent exposure to high-intensity strobes and LED effects; uses protective strategies at work (breaks, dark adaptation, avoiding direct gaze into fixtures) per supervisor policy.

I reviewed Daniel Moore in clinic today. He attended alone. He reports variable daytime alertness, particularly after late finishes at venues, and occasional missed meals when on tour. He notes that colleagues sometimes observe brief staring with eyelid flutter and loss of track of conversation during programming sessions with bright scenes. He keeps a diary and uses a smartwatch, which occasionally flags elevated heart rate preceding events. Sleep is typically 5–6 hours on show days.

Seizure history and recent pattern: He has generalised epilepsy, with probable photosensitive component. In December he had a run of 4 seizures within half an hour (not full generalised tonic-clonic, fluctuating in intensity, resolved without medication). In February there was 4 further seizures at night, and in March another during physiotherapy (unwitnessed by mother). He denies tongue biting or significant injury this year; one scalp bump in December eased with rest and ice. No emergency department attendances.

Current medication: 
- Lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily
- Clobazam 10 mg at night (additional 10 mg PRN for clusters, used twice since January)
- Folic acid 5 mg daily (patient preference)
- Salbutamol inhaler PRN

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Examination today: Alert and oriented. Speech fluent. Cranial nerves normal. No focal neurological deficit. Gait normal. Weight stable. No tremor.

Investigations: Patient reports prior EEG demonstrating generalised spike–wave and photoparoxysmal response at certain flash frequencies; we have requested the formal reports. No recent MRI; not routinely indicated in idiopathic generalised epilepsy, but patient is happy to forgo unless new focal features emerge.

Occupational considerations: We discussed photosensitivity management at work including minimising direct line-of-sight to strobe arrays, using brimmed cap/blue-blocking lenses if helpful, planned breaks, hydration, and sleep hygiene around show days. Colleagues are aware of basic seizure first aid and will maintain a brief witness account when possible.

Plan:
- Continue lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily.
- Trial brivaracetam add-on 50 mg twice daily for two weeks, then 100 mg twice daily if tolerated; advise to stop and contact clinic if marked mood change or dizziness.
- Reserve clobazam 10 mg as cluster rescue as currently used; avoid routine daytime dosing given sedation at work.
- Arrange EEG with photic stimulation at our centre to characterise photoparoxysmal response and guide workplace adjustments; provide written summary for employer if patient consents.
- Provide seizure diary template; encourage smartwatch event tagging to correlate with triggers (strobe sequences, sleep loss, dehydration).
- Safety: avoid working at height alone; ensure spotters present during rigging; maintain hydration; prioritise regular meals; discuss driving status separately according to DVLA regulations if applicable to his licence category.
- Follow-up in 3 months, sooner if clusters increase or if brivaracetam not tolerated.

Thank you for your ongoing care. Please let me know if there are any concerns or if shared monitoring is needed in the interim.

Yours sincerely

Centre for Neurology Services

Neurosciences Division

Clinic Date: 9 July 2019

Dr Priya Shah
Consultant Neurologist
Riverside Neurology Clinic
12 Brook Lane, Manchester M20 5HT

Dear Dr Priya Shah,

Alex Morgan, DOB: 22-09-1987, Hospital No: M843219 NHS No. 6049927713
Flat 3, 27 Willow Court, Manchester M14 2AB

Summary and Background:

I reviewed Alex Morgan in clinic today. The primary carer attended and reported significant fatigue related to round‑the‑clock caregiving responsibilities, including disrupted sleep due to night-time monitoring and coordination of respite arrangements. The caregiving context has been challenging over recent months, and the carer requested documentation to support access to additional respite and workplace flexibility.

Seizure History Since Last Review:

In December 3 generalised tonic-clonic seizures were reported. In March two nocturnal seizures occurred, and in June another during respite care. These events were described by the primary carer and corroborated by respite staff notes in June. There were no reported injuries, tongue bites, or prolonged post‑ictal confusional states requiring emergency services; however, the carer noted marked tiredness for 24–36 hours after each episode.

Current Treatment and Tolerability:

The patient is taking Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily and Levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily as reported by the carer. Adherence is generally good with a weekly pill organiser; one missed evening dose was acknowledged in late May. Side effects reported include intermittent irritability and reduced appetite attributed by the carer to Levetiracetam; no rash or ataxia reported. Vitamin D3 1,000 IU daily continues through primary care.

Aetiology and Investigations:

No new structural aetiology has been identified. A prior MRI (2017) reportedly showed no focal lesion. Routine blood tests arranged by the GP in April (FBC, U&E, LFT, vitamin D) were within reference limits per shared records. The carer requested repeat safety bloods given ongoing fatigue.

Functional and Social Context:

The carer describes cumulative sleep deprivation due to nocturnal monitoring and disrupted routines following the March events. They report resilience but are seeking increased respite frequency and assistance with transport to appointments. The patient engages with a day activity group twice weekly when available.

Risk and Safety:

The carer uses a simple nocturnal alert device and maintains a written seizure log. Post‑ictal supervision is available at home, and rescue medication is not currently prescribed. There is no reported alcohol or recreational drug use. The home environment has been adjusted to reduce fall risk (padded headboard, shower seat). Driving is not undertaken.

Management Plan:

- Continue current Lamotrigine and Levetiracetam at the present doses pending review of adherence and tolerability.
- Arrange serum Lamotrigine and Levetiracetam trough levels, FBC, U&E, LFT, and vitamin D via our phlebotomy clinic.
- Provide a letter supporting the carer’s request for enhanced respite provision and flexibility at work, citing night-time disruption and recent seizure pattern.
- Offer carer support signposting to local services and a fatigue management leaflet; carer accepts.
- Reinforce seizure diary completion, including potential triggers, missed doses, and recovery times.
- Discussed, patient- and carer‑reported: if further events occur, we will consider rationalising therapy and exploring alternative options after blood results and adherence review.
- Follow‑up in 4 months, sooner if there are further convulsive events or concerns from the carer.

Yours sincerely,

Neurosciences Division 

Clinic Date: 24 August 2012 

Dr Helen Morris 
Consultant Neurologist  
Centre for Epilepsy  
King’s College Hospital, Denmark Hill, London SE5 9RS  

Dear Dr Helen Morris, 

Michael Turner, DOB: 22-03-1957, Hospital No: K837461 NHS No. 9083442176  
Flat 2, 14 Brook Lane, London, SE15 3QX  

Diagnosis:

Seizure disorder under active follow‑up; current pattern improving with recent lifestyle changes. Medication response mixed to date.

Aetiology:

No definitive structural cause identified on prior records; historical imaging and bloods unremarkable per patient report. We will verify past results at next review.

Other Medical Problems:

Reports intermittent low back pain related to previous workplace posture; managed with physiotherapy exercises. Vitamin D sufficiency maintained with over‑the‑counter supplementation per GP.

Management Plan:

- Continue current regimen of Lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily and Levetiracetam 750 mg twice daily as tolerated; no brand change requested.  
- Maintain new regular daily routine, with consistent sleep–wake times, which the patient feels has contributed to improvement since retirement.  
- Safety advice reinforced regarding bathing, heights, and operating machinery; driving not undertaken.  
- Arrange serum levels and routine bloods at next visit; consider cautious dose rationalisation if stability persists.  
- Review in six months or sooner if relapse.

Clinical Summary:

Since retiring earlier this year, he has adopted a more regular routine with fixed sleep and meal times, and he reports a noticeable improvement in overall stability, energy, and recovery after episodes. In March he had a run of six seizures within half an hour (not full generalised tonic-clonic, fluctuating in intensity, resolved without medication). In June there was two further seizures at night, and in August another during physiotherapy (unwitnessed by mother). He describes these as shorter and less disruptive than prior years, with quicker return to baseline and no injuries. There have been no emergency department visits, no use of rescue medication, and no missed doses. He and his family feel the new routine post‑retirement has helped.

Examination today was unremarkable with stable observations. Mood and sleep quality have improved, and he is engaging in light exercise under physiotherapy guidance without post‑event sequelae. We discussed that while episodes have occurred, the trend appears favourable, and we will aim for continued stability before contemplating any medication adjustments.

Yours sincerely

Department of Neurology 

Clinic Date: 21 September 2025 

Dr Patel  
St. George’s University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust  
Department of Neurology, Blackshaw Road, London SW17 0QT  

Dear Dr Patel,  

Emily Carter, DOB: 14-03-1991, Hospital No: H392847 NHS No. 9045127731  
22 Willow Bank, Tooting, London SW17 8EP 

Diagnoses: 

Recurrent seizures of uncertain classification. Prior event during air travel (reported 2023). 

Current Medication: 

Levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily  
Clobazam 10 mg nocte as required for clusters 

Plan: 

- Continue Levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily.  
- Clobazam 10 mg at night used sparingly for short periods during higher-risk weeks; patient advised to avoid daytime sedation when travelling.  
- Arrange repeat ambulatory EEG and MRI with epilepsy protocol given persisting episodes and historical in-flight event.  
- Seizure and trigger diary to continue; patient has agreed to record sleep, stress levels, and travel exposure.  
- Discussed aviation-related anxiety; offered referral to clinical psychology for travel anxiety management.  
- Safety advice reinforced (bathing supervision, heights, machinery, and adherence to DVLA guidance).  
- Follow-up in 4 months or sooner if escalation occurs. 

I reviewed Emily Carter in clinic today. She reports a longstanding history of episodic events, with a notable previous seizure occurring during air travel; she describes significant anticipatory anxiety around flying since then. There is no clear precipitant beyond sleep disruption and travel-related stress, and there are no consistent focal warnings reported. 

Over the past year seizure control has been relatively stable. She experiences two generalised tonic-clonic seizures every 2 months. Absence seizures remain infrequent, usually no more than twice weekly, and myoclonic jerks are reported only occasionally in the mornings. She keeps a detailed diary which broadly supports this pattern, with clusters sometimes following long-haul flights or nights of poor sleep. 

She previously trialled Lamotrigine (titrated to 150 mg twice daily) but discontinued due to rash and dizziness. She also had a brief trial of Topiramate (up to 50 mg twice daily) which was stopped for cognitive slowing. She feels Levetiracetam has been better tolerated overall, with occasional irritability that she manages through exercise and structured routines. 

We discussed strategies to mitigate travel-related triggers including sleep prioritisation, hydration, avoiding alcohol, and using aisle seats to reduce stress. She expresses interest in graded exposure and psychological support to address her travel anxiety, which I believe is appropriate. 

I will update you following the planned investigations and our next review. Please feel free to contact me if there are any concerns in the interim. 

With best wishes,

Clinic Date: 23 September 2023 

Dr Amelia Shah 
Consultant Neurologist  
Centre for Epilepsy

Dear Dr Amelia Shah, 

Ms Hannah Keane, DOB: 22-03-1992, Hospital No: K847201 NHS No. 9087712345  
12 Rowan Close, Croydon, CR0 6JP  

Diagnosis: 

Focal epilepsy with concurrent absence and myoclonic phenomena reported in history; current management focused on focal onset events

Aetiology: 

Non-lesional MRI; no structural substrate identified; perinatal and developmental history unremarkable

Other Medical Problems: 

Generalised anxiety symptoms under community psychological support; iron deficiency corrected; no current cardiac or endocrine issues

Management Plan: 

- Continue Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily as monotherapy for focal epilepsy.
- Maintain single-manufacturer brand to avoid bioavailability variation.
- Rescue plan unchanged: buccal midazolam 10 mg for any convulsive seizure lasting >5 minutes or seizure clusters as per prior protocol; carer trained and confident.
- Bloods today: FBC, U&E, LFTs for routine monitoring; lamotrigine level not routinely required unless clinical change.
- Safety: reinforced SUDEP and medication adherence discussion; advised adequate sleep and hydration.
- Driving: not driving and remains counseled per DVLA guidance.
- Follow-up: review in 6 months; earlier if escalation in frequency, injury, or medication intolerance.

Background and Current Status: 

I reviewed Ms Hannah Keane in clinic today accompanied by her primary carer, who reports increasing fatigue related to caregiving responsibilities, particularly overnight supervision. Over the past year seizure control has been relatively stable. She experiences four generalised tonic-clonic seizures every 2 months. Absence seizures remain infrequent, usually no more than twice weekly, and myoclonic jerks are reported only occasionally in the mornings. From a focal epilepsy perspective, her semiology remains consistent with focal onset seizures with preserved awareness progressing on occasion to behavioural arrest; there has been no new aura evolution. There have been no injuries, status episodes, or emergency attendances. Medication adherence is good, and there are no significant adverse effects beyond mild morning nausea that settles with food.

Caregiving Context: 

The primary carer’s fatigue is impacting household routine and may reduce nocturnal observation reliability. We discussed pragmatic adjustments: use of a bed alarm, rotating rest periods, and linking with local carers’ support for respite options. The carer will liaise with the GP regarding a carers’ assessment and potential short-break services. We agreed that any deterioration in carer capacity or breakthrough convulsive clusters should prompt early contact with our service.

Yours sincerely

Centre for Epilepsy

Neurosciences Division 

Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 

Dr Amrita Chawla  
Centre for Epilepsy  
Queen Square, London WC1N 3BG  

Dear Dr Amrita Chawla,

Emily Carter, DOB: 23-11-1992, Hospital No: H382910 NHS No. 8472195630  
Flat 5, 28 Clerkenwell Road, London EC1M 5LE  

Generalised Epilepsy

Medication: Ongoing Sodium Valproate since 2021; Levetiracetam added March 2024

Current regimen:
- Sodium Valproate 500 mg in the morning and 1000 mg at night
- Levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily

Therapeutic monitoring:
- Valproate level (trough): 68 mg/L on 20 September 2025 (local reference 50–100 mg/L)
- Full blood count and liver function tests within normal limits (20 September 2025)

Seizures:
Over the past year seizure control has been relatively stable. She experiences 3 generalised tonic-clonic seizures every three months. Absence seizures remain infrequent, usually no more than twice weekly, and myoclonic jerks are reported only occasionally in the mornings.

Clinic summary:
I reviewed Emily Carter today in the neurology clinic for follow‑up of her generalised epilepsy. She reports good adherence to medication, using a weekly pill organiser. Triggers noted include sleep deprivation and missed evening doses; she has been working variable shift patterns which occasionally affect sleep. There have been no injuries, tongue bites are rare, and recovery time post‑GTC is typically 30–45 minutes with residual fatigue for the remainder of the day. She has not required emergency rescue medication over the past six months. No auras are described, and there are no focal features reported by her partner during witnessed events.

She does not drive and is aware of DVLA guidance. No current pregnancy plans; contraception is managed via copper IUD. We discussed SUDEP risk in the context of generalised epilepsy and the importance of maintaining regular sleep and adherence; she has consented to receive written information. She prefers to continue the current regimen as she feels the overall pattern is manageable and the adverse effects are minimal (occasional mild tremor with valproate; no mood changes on levetiracetam).

Plan:
- Continue Sodium Valproate 500 mg morning / 1000 mg night and Levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily.
- Reinforce sleep hygiene and dose‑timing strategies around shift work; patient will liaise with employer regarding more stable shifts where possible.
- Provide patient information leaflets on SUDEP and seizure first aid.
- Safety: continue to avoid driving; maintain seizure diary.
- Bloods: repeat valproate level, FBC and LFTs in 6 months or sooner if clinical change.
- Follow‑up in clinic in 6 months, earlier if seizure frequency increases or adverse effects emerge.

Yours sincerely

King's College Hospital 

Department of Neurosciences 

Clinic Date: 02 September 2014 

Dr Priya Nair
Consultant Neurologist  
King's College Hospital  
Department of Neurosciences, King's College Hospital, London SE5 9RS  

Dear Dr Priya Nair
Consultant Neurologist,  

Samuel Carter, DOB: 14-03-1982, Hospital No: K872319 NHS No. 9076543321  
12 Hawthorn Close, London, SE15 3LP

Thank you for your referral. I reviewed him in our neurology clinic with his sister participating via scheduled speakerphone at his request, as he reports hearing difficulty and finds this format most comfortable for communication and clarification. He attended promptly and engaged well with questions when supported by his family member on the call.

From the history provided by the patient and his sister, He continues to suffer focal aware seizures two to three times per week, mostly in the evenings, though they are brief and self-terminating. No generalised convulsions have been documented in the past twelve months. The family consider his current control satisfactory. There are occasional prompts from his sister to sit and rest when an event is sensed, and he typically resumes normal activity shortly afterwards without a prolonged post-event phase. He denies injuries, tongue biting, or incontinence, and there have been no emergency presentations this year. Sleep is generally adequate, and alcohol intake is minimal. He reports that missed meals and prolonged screen time in the evening may precede events.

He is currently taking Brivaracetam 100 mg twice daily without reported adverse effects. He prefers stability for now and declined any immediate medication adjustments, wishing instead to maintain a consistent routine and continue family-assisted monitoring. We discussed options for future review should the pattern change, and he agreed to keep a brief diary of event times and potential triggers, which he and his sister can complete together during speakerphone check-ins.

On examination today, he was alert and oriented, with normal speech content and no focal neurological deficits. Cardiovascular and general observations were unremarkable. There were no safeguarding concerns. He is not driving and confirms awareness of DVLA guidance as previously documented.

Plan: 
- Continue current antiseizure regimen as tolerated. 
- Family-supported event diary to be maintained; we will review frequency and any functional impact at follow-up. 
- Arrange routine follow-up in six months, with provision for earlier telephone review via scheduled speakerphone if the pattern worsens or if there are new features such as loss of awareness with injuries. 

Thank you for your ongoing care. Please let me know if there are specific questions you would like us to address at the next review.

Yours sincerely

Clinic Date: 14 May 2016 

Dr Wang
Saffron Park Hospital

Saffron Park, London, E14 7JL
Dear Dr Wang
John Doe, DOB: 21-11-1982, Hospital No: P546484 NHS No. 5484656746
Flat 15 Roundwood Road, London, E14 7JL 

Thank you for referring the above patient for review in the Neurology Clinic today for pre-conception counselling in the context of an established seizure disorder. I last reviewed him approximately six months ago, at which point we agreed a period of treatment stability while he and his partner considered pregnancy planning.

He reports stable seizure control since that review. He continues to suffer focal aware seizures four to five times per week, mostly in the evenings, though they are brief and self-terminating. No generalised convulsions have been documented in the past twelve months. The family consider his current control satisfactory. He is keeping a diary and his descriptions are consistent across entries.

Current medicines: Lamotrigine 150 mg b.d., Levetiracetam 1000 mg b.d., and Clobazam 10 mg nocte. He previously trialled Topiramate (discontinued due to cognitive slowing) and Carbamazepine (stopped because of rash), and has not required rescue medication for over a year. He denies adverse effects from his current regimen other than occasional fatigue late in the day. He does not drive and avoids alcohol. Sleep is generally adequate though he notes that missed meals and late nights can precipitate brief events.

Today’s consultation focused on pre-conception considerations. He and his partner are planning to conceive in the coming year. We discussed medication stability prior to conception, the importance of adherence, and general wellbeing measures. He understands that any medication changes are best avoided close to conception unless clinically necessary, and that optimisation should ideally occur several months in advance. He will continue folic acid as per local guidance, commenced by his GP last month. We also discussed safety planning at home, seizure first aid for his partner, and the value of ongoing seizure diaries. He prefers to defer any dose adjustments for now given the acceptable balance of control and tolerability, and will contact us promptly if there is any change.

Plan:
- Continue current antiepileptic regimen unchanged for the present, with emphasis on adherence and consistent routines.
- Maintain folic acid as initiated by primary care and continue general pre-conception health measures.
- Continue seizure diary; report any increase in frequency, changes in semiology, or emergence of adverse effects.
- Provide written information about pre-conception and perinatal considerations in the context of a seizure disorder.
- Arrange follow-up in four months, or sooner if concerns arise.

I will keep you updated following his next review. Please let me know if there are any queries or if further information would be helpful.

Yours sincerely
